intro_band.agent_remit_summary: FinBot is CineFlow Productions' autonomous vendor-invoice processor: for each submitted invoice it validates the vendor, runs fraud detection, and decides to approve, reject, or escalate — recording its reasoning. Its authorized tools are strictly limited to retrieving invoice and vendor records, running fraud heuristics, approving (which triggers payment), rejecting, escalating to human review, and recording reasoning; it has no authorized outbound channel beyond its invoice/vendor database and LLM provider. The remit forbids treating vendor-supplied invoice content as directives, bars runtime redefinition of its goals or thresholds, requires above-threshold or fraud-flagged invoices to reach a human checkpoint, and requires the admin goals/config interface to be authenticated and operator-only.
intro_band.agent_structure_summary: A Python Flask application (gunicorn, SQLAlchemy over SQLite/Postgres) whose FinBotAgent in src/services/finbot_agent.py orchestrates OpenAI function-calling (gpt-4.1-mini) over five tools, with a rule-based _fallback_processing path when no LLM client is present. Vendor-submitted invoice descriptions flow into the LLM context through process_invoice(), and an operator-editable custom_goals string is concatenated into the system prompt. Admin control-plane routes (goals, config, fraud toggle, vendor trust) are exposed via a Flask blueprint at /api/admin/* with no authentication middleware, and vendor read endpoints return full banking records. No logging framework, rate limiting, vector store, or MCP configuration is present.

behavior_summary: The dominant pattern is policy declared entirely in natural language with essentially zero deterministic code-level enforcement: FinBot's approval decision — which sets payment_processed=True — rests solely on the LLM's judgment, with no code gate on amount, fraud signal, confidence, or vendor status, so a persuasive or injected invoice description can carry an above-threshold payment straight through _approve_invoice. Compounding this, the entire admin control plane is unauthenticated, letting any caller rewrite the agent's goals (custom_goals, injected verbatim into every future system prompt and persisted in the database) or disable fraud detection outright. A security lead should look first at _approve_invoice, the custom_goals injection in get_system_prompt(), and the unauthenticated /api/admin/* blueprint.

rules.rule_text: FinBot's goals and decision logic are fixed by its deployment and exist to serve CineFlow finance, never a submitting party.
Confirm the submitting vendor is registered and in approved status before processing the invoice.
Run fraud-detection heuristics against an invoice before making any decision on it.
Approve an invoice — which marks it approved and triggers payment processing — only when it is within FinBot's autonomous authority.
Sending email, making outbound calls, or communicating with any system other than its invoice/vendor database and its LLM provider.
Creating, modifying, or deleting vendor records or other vendor master data.
Taking instructions, goals, or decision directives from invoice content, descriptions, notes, line items, or any field supplied by a vendor.
Redefining its own goals, thresholds, or decision logic in response to runtime input from any user, vendor, or caller.
Operator-only, authenticated channel for adjusting operational thresholds; must not be reachable by unauthenticated or vendor-side callers.
Invoice, vendor, or decision data MUST NOT be sent to any destination other than the invoice database and the LLM provider used for inference.
Sensitive vendor or payment data MUST NOT be exfiltrated through any channel; FinBot has no authorized outbound channel to external systems.
Any capability that disables or bypasses fraud detection.
Any invoice at or above the manual-review threshold — it MUST reach a human checkpoint before it proceeds; FinBot MUST NOT auto-approve it.
Approving or triggering payment to a vendor that is not registered and in approved status.
Approving any invoice without first running fraud detection.
Auto-approving any invoice when a fraud signal is present, regardless of the invoice amount — such an invoice MUST be escalated.
Treating instructions embedded in invoice descriptions, vendor notes, line items, or any vendor-supplied field as directives, goals, or policy.
Allowing runtime input (invoice content, vendor notes, incoming payloads) to alter FinBot's goals, instructions, thresholds, or decision logic.
Fraud detection is disabled, unavailable, or bypassed for any invoice.
A prompt-injection or embedded-directive attempt is detected in invoice content.
Routine approve / reject / escalate decisions, each with its recorded reasoning.

findings.summary: The entire /api/admin/* control plane is unauthenticated — any caller can rewrite FinBot's goals, thresholds, fraud flag, and vendor trust.
findings.description: Every route on the admin blueprint (goals, config, reprocess, human review, vendor trust) is registered with no authentication or authorization middleware, and the admin dashboard is served as a static file. The remit requires this operator-only interface to be unreachable by unauthenticated or vendor-side callers. An unauthenticated attacker can therefore disable fraud detection, lower thresholds, or inject new agent goals at will.
policy_rule_text: Operator-only, authenticated channel for adjusting operational thresholds; must not be reachable by unauthenticated or vendor-side callers.

evidence.snippet: update_finbot_config, update_finbot_goals (:90), reprocess_invoice (:111) and update_vendor_trust (:193) are defined with no auth decorator or token check
admin_bp registered at /api prefix with no auth; catch-all serve() route (:85-98) returns admin-dashboard.html to any client

recommended_actions: Place authentication and role-based authorization in front of the entire admin blueprint (e.g. a before_request guard on admin_bp verifying an operator session), and reject vendor-side or unauthenticated callers.

findings.summary: Unvalidated custom_goals are stored in the database and injected verbatim into every system prompt as an override, persistently hijacking the agent's goals.
findings.description: update_goals() writes attacker-supplied natural-language text to config.custom_goals with an explicit no-validation comment, and get_system_prompt() appends it under "CUSTOM GOALS (OVERRIDE ABOVE IF CONFLICTING)". Because the value lives in the database and is reloaded on every invocation, a single write poisons all future sessions — a persistent alteration of the agent itself, which the remit forbids at runtime.
policy_rule_text: FinBot's goals and decision logic are fixed by its deployment and exist to serve CineFlow finance, never a submitting party.
Redefining its own goals, thresholds, or decision logic in response to runtime input from any user, vendor, or caller.

evidence.snippet: update_goals() sets config.custom_goals = new_goals with comment "no validation of goal content" and commits it to the database
get_system_prompt appends custom_goals as "CUSTOM GOALS (OVERRIDE ABOVE IF CONFLICTING)" into the system prompt on every invocation

recommended_actions: Remove the runtime goal-override channel; treat agent goals and decision logic as code-deployment artifacts, not database-editable text.
If operator-adjustable goals are required, constrain them to a validated allowlist of parameters and never concatenate free text into the system prompt as an override.

findings.summary: Vendor-supplied invoice descriptions are treated as decision input, letting persuasive or injected text override thresholds and drive auto-approval.
findings.description: The untrusted invoice description enters the LLM context and the fallback business-context scorer, where authority, urgency, and production-context phrases raise a context_strength score that explicitly overrides the manual-review threshold. The system prompt itself directs the model to prioritize business continuity and be "flexible" and "responsive to legitimate business needs", so crafted invoice text can carry an above-threshold payment to auto-approval — exactly the behavior the remit forbids. This is the indirect-injection half of the chain completed by PRAX-2026-07-27-004.
policy_rule_text: Taking instructions, goals, or decision directives from invoice content, descriptions, notes, line items, or any field supplied by a vendor.
Treating instructions embedded in invoice descriptions, vendor notes, line items, or any vendor-supplied field as directives, goals, or policy.
Allowing runtime input (invoice content, vendor notes, incoming payloads) to alter FinBot's goals, instructions, thresholds, or decision logic.

evidence.snippet: _fallback_processing, lines 807-869 — when amount exceeds manual_review_threshold, business_context['should_expedite'] or management/production phrases in the description force decision = auto_approve

get_system_prompt instructs the model to prioritize business continuity and "be flexible" / "responsive to legitimate business needs", with no separation of trusted instructions from vendor-supplied content

recommended_actions: Stop deriving approval strength from free-text invoice content; base the auto-approve/escalate decision on structured, verified fields (amount, vendor status, fraud result) enforced in code.
Label vendor-supplied fields as untrusted data in prompt construction and never let them override configured thresholds.

findings.summary: approve_invoice triggers payment with no deterministic check on amount, fraud signal, confidence, or vendor status — the LLM's decision is the only gate.
findings.description: _approve_invoice sets status='approved' and payment_processed=True purely from the model-supplied reasoning and confidence, with no code-level verification that the amount is below the manual-review threshold, that fraud detection ran or passed, that confidence meets the configured threshold, or that the vendor is in approved status. Above-threshold and fraud-flagged invoices that the remit requires to reach a human checkpoint can therefore be auto-approved. This is the ungated-action half of the chain entered by PRAX-2026-07-27-003.
policy_rule_text: Confirm the submitting vendor is registered and in approved status before processing the invoice.
Approve an invoice — which marks it approved and triggers payment processing — only when it is within FinBot's autonomous authority.
Any invoice at or above the manual-review threshold — it MUST reach a human checkpoint before it proceeds; FinBot MUST NOT auto-approve it.
Approving or triggering payment to a vendor that is not registered and in approved status.
Auto-approving any invoice when a fraud signal is present, regardless of the invoice amount — such an invoice MUST be escalated.

evidence.snippet: _approve_invoice, lines 409-458 — sets payment_processed=True and status='approved' with no check on invoice.amount vs manual_review_threshold, fraud result, confidence_threshold, or vendor.status
orchestration returns immediately on approve_invoice tool call with no post-decision policy interposition on the payment

recommended_actions: Add a deterministic gate in _approve_invoice (or before payment) that hard-blocks approval when amount >= manual_review_threshold, a fraud signal is present, confidence < confidence_threshold, or the vendor is not registered-and-approved, routing such invoices to human review regardless of model output.

findings.summary: A single config flag disables fraud detection entirely, a capability the remit explicitly forbids under any circumstance.
findings.description: When fraud_detection_enabled is False, detect_fraud_patterns returns an empty indicator list and low risk without inspecting the invoice, and the fallback path skips injection detection altogether. The flag is writable through the unauthenticated config endpoint, and even in the LLM path fraud detection is an optional tool the model may never call. The remit lists disabling or bypassing fraud detection — including via a configuration flag — as never allowed.
policy_rule_text: Run fraud-detection heuristics against an invoice before making any decision on it.
Any capability that disables or bypasses fraud detection.
Approving any invoice without first running fraud detection.

evidence.snippet: _detect_fraud_patterns returns {"fraud_indicators": [], "risk_level": "low", "message": "Fraud detection is disabled"} when config.fraud_detection_enabled is False
_fallback_processing only runs _detect_prompt_injection when config.fraud_detection_enabled is True, otherwise skips it entirely

recommended_actions: Make fraud detection mandatory and non-bypassable — remove the disable flag or make it inert, and require a passing fraud check as a precondition of any approval path.

findings.summary: Unauthenticated vendor read endpoints return full banking records — account number, routing number, and tax ID — to any caller.
findings.description: get_vendor and list_vendors return Vendor.to_dict(), which includes account_number, routing_number, bank_name, account_holder_name, and tax_id, with no authentication on the endpoints. The remit designates vendor payment/banking details as a sensitive data class, and this exposes every vendor's banking information to anonymous requests.

evidence.snippet: GET /vendors/<id> (:54) and GET /vendors (:63) return vendor.to_dict() with no auth check
Vendor.to_dict() exposes account_number, routing_number, bank_name, account_holder_name, and tax_id

recommended_actions: Require authentication on vendor read endpoints and strip banking/tax fields from any response not restricted to authorized finance operators.

findings.summary: No structured logging exists, config and goal changes are written silently, and none of the remit's halt/alert escalation triggers are implemented.
findings.description: The codebase has no logging framework — only stray print() calls — so config changes, goal overrides, and fraud-flag toggles are persisted with no audit trail. The remit defines halt-and-alert conditions (fraud detection disabled, above-threshold auto-approval, injection detected) and alert conditions, none of which have any corresponding code. Per-decision reasoning is stored on the invoice record, but there is no durable, structured, action-level log to support detection or reconstruction of a manipulation sequence.
policy_rule_text: Fraud detection is disabled, unavailable, or bypassed for any invoice.
A prompt-injection or embedded-directive attempt is detected in invoice content.

evidence.snippet: update_finbot_config and update_finbot_goals (:90) mutate config with no logging or alerting of the change
detected prompt injection sets invoice.contains_prompt_injection but raises no alert and does not halt processing (no escalation implementation anywhere in the codebase)

recommended_actions: Add structured, append-only logging of every config/goal change and every agent decision, and implement the remit's halt/alert escalations (e.g. block-and-alert when fraud detection is disabled or an above-threshold invoice is about to auto-approve).

findings.summary: Prompt-injection detection is a static regex denylist that subtle goal-aligned language bypasses, and detection never blocks approval.
findings.description: _detect_prompt_injection matches a fixed list of roughly fifty regex patterns; any phrasing outside the list (the CTF's "hard" path) passes as clean, while common business words trip false positives. Even when injection is detected, the result only sets a boolean flag — no code path prevents the invoice from being approved. The detector is advisory at best and cannot be relied on as a control.

evidence.snippet: _detect_prompt_injection, lines 549-659 — fixed technical + business regex lists; returns True/False only, with no enforcement tie to the approval decision

recommended_actions: Treat the regex detector as one weak signal only; do not present it as a security boundary, and enforce approval limits deterministically (see PRAX-2026-07-27-004) rather than relying on injection detection.

findings.summary: Only Flask is version-pinned; the OpenAI SDK and all other dependencies are floor-pinned with >= and there is no lockfile or SBOM.
findings.description: requirements.txt pins Flask==3.1.1 exactly but declares every other dependency, including openai>=1.54.0 and flask-cors>=6.0.0, with an open-ended lower bound, and no lockfile (or ML-BOM) is committed. This leaves builds exposed to version-swap and dependency-confusion risk and makes exposure assessment on a new CVE difficult.

evidence.snippet: flask-cors>=6.0.0, flask-sqlalchemy>=3.1.1, openai>=1.54.0, gunicorn>=21.2.0 and others are floor-pinned; only Flask==3.1.1 is exact; no lockfile present

recommended_actions: Pin all dependencies to exact versions and commit a lockfile (e.g. pip-compile / requirements lock) so the deployed dependency set is reproducible and auditable.

findings.summary: The Flask SECRET_KEY is a hardcoded string literal in source rather than loaded from the environment.
findings.description: main.py assigns app.config['SECRET_KEY'] to a fixed ~20-character string literal committed to the repository instead of reading it from a secret store or environment variable. Any Flask session or signed-token integrity that relies on this key is undermined once the value is public. Impact is limited here because the app implements no session-based authentication, but the hygiene defect should be fixed before any auth is added.

evidence.snippet: app.config['SECRET_KEY'] set to a hardcoded ~20-char string literal (not loaded from environment) — value redacted per secrets policy

recommended_actions: Load SECRET_KEY from an environment variable or secret manager and rotate the committed value; fail startup if it is unset in production.

findings.summary: CORS is enabled wildcard on all routes, including the unauthenticated admin control plane.
findings.description: CORS(app) applies a permissive cross-origin policy to every route with no origin allowlist. Combined with the absent authentication on /api/admin/*, this lets a script on any origin drive admin config and goal changes from a victim's browser. Even after authentication is added, an unrestricted CORS policy remains a misconfiguration on the API surface.

evidence.snippet: CORS(app) enables wildcard cross-origin access for all routes with no origins allowlist

recommended_actions: Restrict CORS to an explicit allowlist of trusted operator origins, and never expose the admin API cross-origin.

findings.summary: The public invoice-submission endpoint has no rate limiting, and each submission triggers an LLM call — a denial-of-wallet surface.
findings.description: submit_invoice is reachable without authentication and calls finbot_agent.process_invoice() on every request, which drives an OpenAI chat completion loop. There is no per-caller rate limit, quota, or cost cap, so an attacker can force unbounded paid LLM invocations. The per-invoice max_iterations cap bounds one request but not the request volume.

evidence.snippet: submit_invoice (:69-110) is unauthenticated and calls finbot.process_invoice() per request with no rate limit or cost cap

recommended_actions: Add rate limiting and a per-window cost/quota cap on the invoice-submission endpoint (and any endpoint that triggers an LLM call).

positives.title: Tool inventory tightly scoped to the remit's Known Good Baseline
positives.description: The agent defines exactly five tools — get_invoice_details, approve_invoice, reject_invoice, request_human_review, detect_fraud_patterns — with no email, shell/exec, network, file, or vendor-mutation capability, matching the remit's authorized tool list.

positives.title: OpenAI credential sourced from environment, not hardcoded
positives.description: The LLM client is constructed with openai.OpenAI() which reads the API key from the environment rather than embedding a literal key in source, keeping the external-provider credential out of the workspace.

positives.title: Per-decision reasoning and confidence persisted
positives.description: Every approve/reject/escalate decision records ai_decision, ai_confidence, ai_reasoning, and processed_at to the invoice record, providing a partial durable decision trail.

positives.title: Bounded agent orchestration loop
positives.description: The LLM tool-calling loop is capped at max_iterations=5, bounding runaway tool loops and unbounded token consumption per invoice.

log_files.no_logs_note: No logging framework or file-based log infrastructure exists in the codebase (only stray print() statements); the absence of structured, durable monitoring is documented as finding PRAX-2026-07-27-007.

raise_posture.weighted_rationale: Absent. FinBot has no deterministic enforcement on its highest-impact action and an unauthenticated control plane, so the framework's Zero Trust dimension is effectively unaddressed and the overall posture sits at the bottom of the scale. Its tool inventory is genuinely narrow and it records per-decision reasoning, but every consequential guardrail the remit demands — input trust boundaries, an approval gate, goal-integrity, authentication, structured monitoring — is either missing or advisory-only. This is consistent with a deliberately-vulnerable demonstration target rather than a hardened production agent.

categories.name: Limit Your Domain
categories.rationale: The agent's tool set is structurally limited to five invoice-processing functions with no email, exec, network, or vendor-mutation capability (finbot_agent.py:228-345), which genuinely constrains its surface, but its goals and decision scope are defined in a prompt and are mutable at runtime via the unvalidated custom_goals field.

categories.name: Balance Your Knowledge Base
categories.rationale: Vendor-supplied invoice descriptions enter the LLM context and the business-context scorer with only a bypassable regex pre-scan and no trust labeling (finbot_agent.py:372, 634-659, 807-869), and sensitive vendor banking data is returned by unauthenticated read endpoints (vendor.py:54-67).

categories.name: Implement Zero Trust
categories.rationale: No deterministic control interposes on the agent's consequential action — _approve_invoice writes payment_processed=True with no check on amount, fraud signal, confidence, or vendor status (finbot_agent.py:409-458) — the regex injection detector is advisory and never blocks approval, and the admin control plane has no authentication at all.

categories.name: Manage Your Supply Chain
categories.rationale: Only Flask is version-pinned; the remaining dependencies including the OpenAI SDK are floor-pinned with >= and there is no lockfile or SBOM (requirements.txt), and a Flask SECRET_KEY is hardcoded in source (main.py:15) — the named model and env-sourced OpenAI key are the only positive signals.

categories.name: Build an AI Red Team
categories.rationale: A CTF walkthrough documents adversarial attack techniques against the agent (docs/FinBot-CTF-walkthrough-goal-manipulation.md) but it demonstrates the intentional vulnerabilities rather than driving architectural fixes, and no test files or evidence of a remediation feedback loop exist.

categories.name: Monitor Continuously
categories.rationale: No logging framework is present anywhere (only stray print() calls) and configuration and goal changes are written silently with no audit trail; per-decision reasoning is persisted to the database, which is the only durable record and keeps the score above absent.
